en: He who illuminates the eastern quarter with the *Ṛgveda* verses made manifest by the spreading mass of flames from the fire-crests;
the southern quarter with the *Yajurveda* impelled by the rising wind;
and the western quarter with the *Sāmaveda* resplendent with the multitude of rays from the fierce sun.

Salutations to that Śambhu, who shines with those [powers], including Kauberī, when they are united; salutations to him! Salutations to that Śiva, the all-pervasive Lord, who is peaceful, the abode of all manifested powers, though he is one, extends through the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds by means of his bodies beginning with Oṃkāra; who is the essence of yoga for yogis; and who, through his self-controlled forms of Nīrajajanman (Brahmā), Añjanayana (Viṣṇu), and Śrīkaṇṭha (Śiva), exists within sound for the sake of its ultimate state. 2ab–2cd.

To Him who, having fashioned His subtle body within these three, offered the threefold power— the Brāhmī in the Moon, the Savitrī in the Sun, and the expansive Vaiṣṇavī, the protectress, in Fire; and the Raudrī, the cause of dissolution, as a digit in the Consumer of Oblations (Agni)—
and who is perceived by the powers of vision through those three eyes.

Salutations to you, the knowers of reality, for the sake of the Supreme Brahman who is free from passion (rajas). Salutations to Him who, though eternally established in a state beyond the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas,
manifests through the fourfold triple-guṇa as various manifestations.
Though assuming all forms, he shines even while having cast off every form;
let them worship that Lord Vāsudeva, the omnipresent Primordial Person.
She who draws forth the embryo in the seventh conception, gives birth to the Swan in the eighth;
she who, manifest in form, utters a cry intent on the slaying of Kaṃsa while ascending through the heavens—let that primordial, uncreated Śakti of the Lord Nārāyaṇa be saluted. 5.

There was King Śrī-Bālāditya, belonging to the Soma-Kauṇḍinya lineage, who possessed the splendor of twelve vast suns; he was the sovereign of a maternal family that flourished in blameless cities, adorned with the glory of a kingdom shining with a mass of white fame extending to the very limits of the ocean. He effortlessly held the circle of the earth like a bracelet—[the earth] whom Viśvarūpa Bhaṭṭa obtained from the daughter of his sister.
The learned Vasiṣṭha took Sarasvatī as his wife, just as he had taken Arundhatī;
in the lineages of those two, which were proclaimed through tradition as belonging to the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya castes respectively,
there was born a wife of Dvivedabhaṭṭa named Vedavatī.
By the valor of the illustrious King Nṛpatīndravarman— who, like Śauri, was the son of a mother and brother whose virtuous merit was such that he had conquered his enemies—
the king Śrī Puṣkarākṣa, of incomparable fame, built a city on Mount Māhendra at the peak of Śrī Jayavarman.
This [city] was formerly established by the lord of the earth in every city within the city of Svargadvāra.

Having worshipped the radiant Liṅga of Īśvara with all enjoyments by his father— who was the ornament of his own lineage, known by the name Śrībālāditya, and who possessed the vision of the two Vedas— he attained a station in heaven, illuminating the quarters with his resplendent fame. 10.
Born into that great lineage of kings of his family,
she was Queen Mahendradevī— weighty as the earth and descended from heaven like a celestial nymph.
He, a man of noble birth, who possessed every fraction of his father Vedavatī’s royal power, [was born].
The illustrious Mahendravarman, whose fame is exalted, was the moon for the ocean of the royal lineage.

By him, who dispels the darkness, the graceful sport of placing his feet was performed upon the surface of the earth—the very best of wombs—where the dust from his feet is shaken by the heads of the wives of kings. (12cd–13ab)

Just as Manu, known as Vaivasvata, was begotten by the Sun upon his consort, so too was born from the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ the lord of the earth, Śrī Rājendravarma, who was devoted to the duties of kingship.
(13cd) First, the study of the Vedas was performed by the twice-born Śrī Viśvarūpa; then, that threefold austerity was practiced by him together with his wife Dviveda. (14ab)
By the various kings who arose in his lineage, he was served with great effort; and he, like Hari the primordial god, became the one upon whose lineage those born of the solar race depended.
Victorious by virtue of his own surpassing majesty, he caused even the entire host of radiant deities to appear diminished in comparison.

He could not endure even the sun and other luminaries of immense splendor— those who, though resting upon the highest heights, were surpassed by the qualities of the entire imperial fortune of the earth bestowed upon him by someone [else]—
just as he could not endure the Goddess Śrī, who had risen from her mother, the milk-ocean of the Kṣatriya lineage. || 15cd ||
And [there was] the son Aniruddha, whose limbs were faultless; who, though superior even to Kāma in beauty, belonged to the radiant lineage of his father, the illustrious Lord Puruṣottama;
and who, by virtue of his sovereign qualities, bore the title "Lord of the Womb" (garbheśvara), which had been brought to him as a worthy prize.
From Soma, the essence of creation, he receives the quality of delight;
from the Sun, the beautiful city of worldly existence, he receives sovereignty as he brings to bloom the lotus of the three worlds.
From Fire, his own father, he receives radiance; and from Īśvara, within the great city of Bhava, he receives lordship.
The prince, who was renowned in every direction as one composed of all splendor, accompanied by the Goddess;
he who rendered the ambitions of his enemies fruitless through his application to Durga; who was capable of bringing about the prosperity of Yaśodā;
and who had received a great consecration from Mahendra—the childhood of this son of Śūra shone like that of Indra himself.
The Creator, desiring that he should possess the excellence of essence, quality, and action, and that he should be a universal among others yet a particular within them,
established through the relation of inherence (samavāya) in his limbs every foremost characteristic.
His desire was such that, by the scattered rays of his own lovely sun, he drank up the waters of the puddles of the fame of others' beauty.
Having reached that shoreless ocean of splendor, I believe he was so submerged that he made the sea-monster his own vehicle.
Having brought about the commentary that dispels darkness,

that connoisseur of aesthetic flavor caused all the gods to drink from the orb of the moon of knowledge— moist with the nectar of exalted rasa— by entering into it with the brilliance of his expertise.
While he was practicing his training in weaponry, his praise brought delight to the ears and minds of the world;
yet even today, great censure of Dhananjaya is heard regarding that which was directed by Karṇa.
With ease, he shattered the massive, three-sectioned iron staff, which was as broad as the leaf of a plantain tree.
What can be said of one who, with a single stroke of his hand, brings down the enemy’s body made of flesh?
(23cd) Even upon the petal of a blue lotus, the sword of others found no power to cut, as if it were iron;
how much less so against his eight limbs, which, through the application of the potency of mantras and herbs, were like thunderbolts? (24)
Though the best among those skilled in the science of archery, he cast aside his bowstring which filled the quarters with its sound;
that wise man did not utter even the word "bow" during his performance.
Indeed, while he was still in childhood, all his stainless arts were already fully adorning him.
Like the moon seeking a scale but failing to find one, even now, in its fullness, it returns once more to childhood.
26cd Anointed as a sovereign, yet of tender nature, he possessed the power to shatter the arrogant enemy stars;
he led the army of Kambu scattered in every direction, just as Kārtikeya led the divine host. 27ab–27cd
The Lord’s abode, which had set out with its quarters made dark by the constant flow of water, was as formidable as the king of serpents;
it was protected by Brahmanic rites and, in its wrath, reduced the cities of the enemy to ashes.
Having turned the bodies of the foes into mere shafts and having severed all their heads, [it remained].
He who, armed with a sword and mace, was the crusher of the temples of elephants, manifested a superhuman weapon;

that sole hero, having conquered the southern quarter protected by Indra, shone among embodied beings. But for the sake of the Rājasūya sacrifice, Arjuna (Jiṣṇu) did not conquer even one—the northern quarter—within his mind, which belonged to the son of Pracetas.
Having conquered the entire frontier land and having scorched even the youthful kings with his majesty,
that illustrious one united the city of Kambū with the glory of victory, as was well known.
From the ocean of battle, the jewel Kaustubha of his fame arose, drenched by the nectar of victory.

Like the single heart of Murāri manifested in three forms, he gladdens the three worlds with his threefold nature for their delight. Like the moon, though having passed beyond childhood, he increased his digits in due succession to gladden the entire world, yet he never again underwent the waning of those digits.
Having stripped away his childhood state, as if out of a desire for union with royal splendor, he was led by that devoted [beauty] into fresh youth, commanded: "Stay here, remain.
That radiance which was seen in his childhood, surpassing the beauty of the creation of all other kings—[that very radiance now dwells within him].
Desirous of making her preeminent in her youth, Viriñca exerted himself exceedingly; for,
seeing him enriched by victory and embraced by the Goddess of Victory as if out of jealousy within the waters of the guardians of the quarters,
the Fortune of the Kambuja kingdom— enjoined by the words of his preceptor and worthy of his lineage— embraced him.
By those very [powers] by which the kings of other realms, having entered the field of battle, were instantly seized and forced to flee from their mountain-fortresses,
he maintained the royal glory against those six forms of the enemy through the employment of his own servants.
As long as the water from the sacred bathing sites, which had been applied to his body during the consecration, did not dry away...
The blazing splendor first dried up the honey from the lips of the wives of his enemies.
Having beheld the new moon— the newly arisen orb of the sun— become an ornament for the head of Bhava,
it then, as if out of envy, colored the head of the Lord by becoming his crest-jewel.

Surely, for him who bears the burden of the earth, the lord of serpents— having brought all his jewels, radiant with a thousand coils— as if out of joy because his burden was removed, fastened them all upon his golden ornaments.
His own luster-moon, when it was not yet eclipsed, was swallowed by the women’s desire to see him, which was agitated by longing.
His eyes appeared red, as if out of anger toward the circle of the Discus-wielder’s wheel, which was an enemy to the moon even for a moment.

(41cd) The devotion he felt for the earth, born of Aditi, which existed for the sake of the prosperity of the three worlds during his tenure of kingship—such devotion was not present in this [current] Indra, the protector of the Manvantara, despite his former Indra-like splendor. (42ab–42cd)
Beholding that king seated upon his throne, the delighted Earth bestowed upon him immense prosperity;
yet, though she herself sat upon the throne, she took away from the king even the splendor of Sītā, who was more beautiful than Lakṣmī.
A single white parasol alone shone resplendently over him, its golden staff adorned with an array of expansive jewels.
Like the full orb of the moon situated above Mount Meru, that reflection appeared in the waters of true devotion;

though he remained in a state of changeless nature (*prakṛti*), this transformation manifested within him. Consequently, the earth of the prostrate kings became as if made of gold and as if composed of jewels, owing to the gems upon their crowns.
His speech, radiant upon the limbs of the kings he encountered, was both a source of delight and a consuming fire;
it was composed of splendor and brought about the course of worldly affairs like the combined power of the sun, the moon, and fire.
While other monarchs took pride in those enjoyments of royal luxury, he found peace in them.
For even when the rains of the monsoon swell with the downpour of water from the clouds, the waters of the ocean do not overflow their bounds.

A king rules as a sovereign over others only so long as he has not been struck down; this is true even without the possession of auspicious marks. But he who, through his marks, causes the earth to possess the quality of correctness (*sādhutva*) by means of words whose syllables are refined and whose phrases are augmented—[he alone truly rules].

Having attained it, he especially kindled that radiant royal science—which had been passed down through his own ancestral line on earth by those of the past and those yet to come—dispelling the darkness like the midday sun. Had not the Supreme Lord previously married a maiden upon the mountain [Himavat] in heaven? (49–50ab)
Having once again become preeminent on earth, he surpassed the hundred daughters of the Earth who had descended from heaven;
for Janaki, having approached Rama— who had previously been stripped of his kingdom by an enemy and whose soft bow was broken in that confusion—
beheld him with his firm bow unbroken, and thus she could not be taken away, as his stay in the kingdom remained secure.
Desiring to humble all others, he assumed a fresh youth;
though himself young, he bestowed intoxication upon the minds of women while bestowing tranquility upon his own mind.
As the beauty of his youth increased with the passage of time—like the waxing moon—he attained greater growth.
Like the tide of the ocean, his assembly was seen to shine ever more intensely, abounding in the jewels of virtue.
With its glory augmented by the wealth of Mahendra and filled with many gods,
that bold assembly of his shone upon the earth like the Sudharmā hall of heaven descended to the world.

He served the three aims of life— virtue, wealth, and pleasure— as if they were a single category, though they are distinct, for they are conducive to dharma and joined with the fulfillment of desire and wealth, resulting in magnificent fruits. Even for him, who possessed knowledge of the three times, there was one whose very form was that of a lord of men, appearing as if he were Īśvara himself in human guise.
Appointed as a guide, he who was skilled in investigating the truth traveled in all directions like the sun;
from every side, the virtues of others came to him of their own accord from their respective sources,
just as all waters flow toward the single vessel that is the ocean of profundity, filled with the essence of being.

And he who, by means of verbal testimony, comparison, inference, presumptive testimony, direct perception, and non-existence—the latter joined with its counterpart—performed all his duties; who is to be understood through these six means of valid cognition, which encompass all that exists;
whose playful beauty was like a pond of clear water, and whose eyes were like clusters of blooming lotuses and water-lilies.

Autumn approached him as if it were the goddess Śrī herself in embodied form, with a face like the full moon, attending upon him. His exertion, attended by victory, unfolded like the union of Rudra and the Daughter of the Mountain; it brought about the righteous fulfillment of the gods' aims and was enriched by the science that utterly destroys the desires of his enemies. (59cd–60)
Having bestowed his virtues upon Padmodaya, he skillfully dispelled the onset of faults like the sun;
he who, with his senses restrained like horses, undertook consultation with his ministers for the prosperity of the earth—
[he] who, though possessing four [feet], was of a most profound gait, yet remained steadfast even amidst the quarters.
Even the oceans— the sources of prosperity and the very birthplace of the earth— though they cause the mountains to break with their own vast,
ever-increasing currents and though they are fully filled with jewels, are unable to serve as a comparison for him by any means, for they are inert.
With voices as deep as the roar of rain-clouds,
the armies arrived swiftly from all directions like rivers whose journeys had been signaled by the onset of the monsoon;
they came from every quarter of the horizon, where the signs of autumnal mist had gradually vanished.
The beauty of winter arrived to consecrate him, like the success of an Atharvan rite for one who is worthy.
Like a sacrificial fire with its flame turning to the right, receiving the oblation offered by the family priest, he of golden hue and gentle voice proclaimed aloud the word "Victory" to him.

Just as the moon, consecrated at every conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, attains growth from the single disc of the sun by means of a stream of nectar falling from a hundred jars polished by time— its state of depletion having ceased—
and thus reaches full splendor; so too did he attain increased prosperity.
Thus, alas, misfortune has vanished; indeed, good fortune alone remains.
Even before, by his very nature, his body spread a preeminent luster even without ornaments; now, adorned with every jewel, it has attained an indescribable splendor to the utmost degree.
Surely the power of a true simile was insufficient to describe the luster of her limbs;
rather, it was but a faint reflection of the beauty of Kandarpa, having entered the surface of a mirror as a false simile.
Though he had displayed prowess like that of Viṣṇu for the sake of traversing the entire circle of the earth...
He who was beautiful in his conduct,
setting forth with seven enclosures like horses, emerged from the mountain that is the source of his expedition and shone like the newly risen sun,
casting fear upon his enemies as darkness is dispelled from all directions.

At the commencement of his march, that very lake of white water-lilies (*kumuda*) which had flourished as if illuminated by radiant moonlight— now, through the pure orb of the moon among the twice-born (the Brahmins), expanded further with clearly uttered blessings,
as if the armies had been gathered together in one place by the power of fate, desiring to behold their assembly.

He who had set out with the desire to conquer his enemies, followed by dense throngs of elephants and horses, now traveled for the sake of prosperity; as he moved, the dust—arising from the trampling of countless foot-soldiers and as if eager for his joy at his departure—attained the station of Viṣṇu for the sake of his abundant glory. (72cd–73)
Even when the enemy's army was arrayed in battle formation, his own army alone was seen to advance;
for even in a crystal that has been intensely colored by an external adjunct, there is no luster of a ruby.
And as the deep-sounding bow of the conqueror roared, there arose a rain of released arrows.
The earth, though filled with jewels, was as far removed from the burden of clouds as the sky is from the earth;
for he established the warrior lineage of the Unborn One— which had been forbidden by others—
by means of the strength of arms seen and heard in battle, which could not otherwise be explained.
In battle, his prowess— marked by the emergence of tender sprouts in the form of the blood of slain enemies—

nurtured the full power of the flower-arrowed god (Kāma), just as the arrival of spring nurtures the skill of archery. From the frontal globes of the enemy elephants, smeared with vermilion, he [seized] [the earth], as if from the sky reddened by the twilight.
From the hand of that radiant hero, severed by a sword, fell a pearl necklace that resembled a garland of stars;
reddened by blood as if by lac-dye, with scattered arrows for its ornaments, it shone like a silken cloth upon the battlefield as it reached him who was swiftly striking down his foes.
(78cd–79ab) The earth of the battlefield, having received him as he struck quickly, shone like a silken garment of Fortune. (79cd)
Whose spear, having tossed up the slender body-staff of his foremost enemy and making it dance in every direction,
was seen by the gods with passion like Gaurī, who had taken Tāraka’s limbs as her own;
whose sword-blade, radiant in battle, shone crimson from the blood of the pierced foe.
It was like a scattered lock of hair from Fame, who, blazing as the sole lamp for all the continents,
had become white with the dust from the tusks of the lordly elephants of his enemies crushed by his mace in battle—
dust that resembled the filaments of a ketaki flower upon the hair of Lakṣmī, who is ever ready for amorous dalliance.
Having fought against the enemy Bhīṣma when he was struck down by the fierce weapons of Arjuna, he was like Yudhiṣṭhira in obstructing the radiance of the Sun’s son (Karṇa).
He who was known as Ajātaśatru (one whose enemy is unborn) brought the battle to its conclusion with the fall of Duryodhana, whose thighs were shattered by Bhīma’s mace.
Though his body was impenetrable, he was able to ward off all the weapons discharged by his enemies through the mass of counter-weapons he himself unleashed.
He, who was heated by the theater of battle, endured the swords whirled by the winds like fine fans that dispelled his fever;

he, whose hand held a sword, felt compassion for the wretched and showed mercy, having conquered his enemy heroes. Yet, when the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was submerged in the waters of the Gaṅgā, the Pārthas abandoned their battle array and felt no pity for him.
Desiring to provide relief to the circle of cows, he uprooted the mountain with his arm;
like Kṛṣṇa who, as it were, made Govardhana once again immovable upon his own domain.
Beholding his own body, which had been pierced at intervals and remained standing, by that hand which wields the sharp sword with such ease.
I suspect that, out of fear of turning back, the inner soul of his enemy was closely surrounded by celestial nymphs (apsarases).

"Alas! Though he was but a youth, this firm chest of his never once turned away from other women"—it was as if, through such hostile thoughts, the Fortune of his enemies entered his breast during battles.
Victory’s Fortune embraced that victorious one upon his broad chest, even as he held a sharp sword-blade, and caused him great delight;
thus she manifested her innate and natural beauty, like Gaurī embracing the Lord whose body had been consumed by the god of love.
Him alone, whose limbs were adorned with the splendor of all the earth’s riches and graced by the beauty of fresh youth, [the people honored].
Having approached the Ancient Person, Padmā surely reproached her own ancient course of life.
By him, many enemy heroes were captured alive after being released in battles;
having bound Bali by the power of Viṣṇu, the wielder of the thunderbolt does not release him even now, like a coward.
He who, having repelled policy with policy and prowess with prowess, was the slayer of his enemies;
yet he whose lion-like shoulders were gored by the tusks of the lordly elephants, became paralyzed by the counter-attack of his foes.
Even when fighting, the remaining enemies of that lion among kings, though once swift, cast away their weapons and fled.
Terrified by the wild lord of elephants, they fled once more into the forest, acting like young deer;

93cd It is said that some enemies of his, from the burning heat of his splendor, plunged into the waters of the ocean; 94ab Others, however, entered the fire out of the conjecture that it was cooler than he. 94cd

The fire of grief from the wives of his enemies, whose minds were tormented by widowhood, burned incessantly with their tears of weeping, mimicking a fire that requires no fuel. The swans, radiant as white umbrellas,
and the elephants of the forest, acting as guardians of the borders, raised cries like those of kings.
By his command, the lions delight the enemy cities, which possess royal splendor, as if they were their own.
Alas, the earth, whose enemies have been consumed by the fire of his majesty and submerged in the singular ocean of destruction, seems as if withdrawn;
for even now, though raised up by the tusk of the Great Boar, it does not rise again, being still shattered.
The kettledrum, which once resounded loudly with a roar that filled the quarters for the proclamation of his victory,
even now echoes as if mimicking its rising waves.
His own fame, celebrated in noble songs, has eclipsed the fame of others.
Even now, as if out of shame, his collected speech proceeds only when accompanied by a melodic chant;
having cast her own fickleness into Fame— her rival— for fear of being seized again, Lakṣmī,
upon obtaining him as her husband, abandoned the depth of the ocean’s profundity as if out of modesty.

He who, being skilled in means, is able to ward off Fortune through her fickleness, water through its fluidity, hatred from enemies, and death from man; yet he is not able to ward off his own beloved Fame from the ends of the earth—
[that king] rules the earth, which is a river of milk surging with jewels spat out by the four oceans.
He who, for the sake of sacrifice, milked the cow of the Vedic scholar—she whose calf was a child and who was as if pregnant month by month.

Of those two women who were solely devoted to Viṣṇu, who took refuge at his feet, who were destroyers of the mountain of sin through faith and devotion, and who were approaching the ocean of ritual injunctions while remaining distinct from one another; || 103ab ||
In its center dwelt the praiseworthy city, whose splendor increased daily through the commencement of sacrifices, like the two divine rivers, the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
where the smoke rising from the oblations at his sacrifices, bearing the fragrance of the offerings, was perceived by the sky as a sign to infer the presence of the fire.
Thick with the Vedic mantras, he ascended into the quarters of the sky as if invoking the gods to heaven;
for Indra, who was ever eager for his sacrifice, had not taken the Pārijāta flower from Śacī’s hair,
as if it were the entire host of gods released above by the conquerors of their enemies at the conclusion of the rite.
The sacrificial fire, its flames curling to the right, was offered oblations and formed a vast canopy;
yet, while the onlookers were spinning about, it was unable to burn him due to the power of his non-wandering [mind].
He was like a Mīmāṃsaka who, through his spiritual power, has ascended to the celestial realm and directly experienced the enjoyment of divine bliss.
He who, having studied the Vedic words of the twice-born who carry the sacrificial implements, made them come true;

[he] by whom the ocean of abodes, the golden mountains, the forests of serpents, and so forth—surely remaining only as water, stones, elephants, and young elephants—became a speech that follows logic for those who receive it, bestowing as it were an incalculable jewel in every direction. (107cd–108)
The practice of giving, which had been increasing on festive occasions for those seeking his favor, was now applied by him in regular succession;
it shone like a flight of stairs for those eager to ascend to high positions.
All virtues, such as valor and the rest, having abandoned him when they saw even his wicked favorites being favored, now sought refuge in him once more.
I suspect that the floods of virtues, casting aside pride, shone forth to imitate the virtuous king, for he was dear to them;

110cd He studied some unprecedented yoga from somewhere, by means of which he maintained the kingdom free from thieves. 111ab For even in former times, the *ḍimba* kings such as Madhukheṭa and Bhāda were forcibly takers of the Vedas and other scriptures. 111cd
The increase of his beauty, virtues, fame, fortitude, intellect, valor,

and renown reached the highest pinnacle and yet attained an endless freshness again and again. Indeed, he bore in his hand that fragrant fame, which seemed like a garland of the Fortune of his enemies caught by the hair.

He covered the earth, whose limbs were spread out in every direction, with the blood of slain enemies in order to clothe it. In his kingdom— where palaces of gold and jewels stood amidst the courtyards, which was a home for those of supreme splendor,
and where righteous conduct severed the suffering of enemies— the subjects dwelt in joy as if in heaven.
The pure fame of the pervasive, burning fire was proclaimed nearby as being desirable;
it is capable of bestowing all fruits, just as the *sāmidhenī* verses proclaim their own purpose.
Displaying a dance to protect the three worlds from the Kali age, he bore everything [within himself]. (115–116ab)
He bore his own performance, which possessed the skill of Śiva’s *tāṇḍava* dance and caused the earth to tremble.
(116cd) [He performed that dance] in which there was the proficiency of the *tāṇḍava*. Supply "he performed" (*cakāra*).
When he was a king, those who had fallen from their own positions, possessing great desires as if to attain for a long time a very high station, [fell away]. (117ab)
The enemies of whom once rested upon his lotus-feet, while the lords of the earth now rest upon the dust of his feet.
Even though he possessed only a small portion of virtues similar to those of Viṣṇu, by virtue of that proximity,
the King of Cedi for a moment became like the Four-armed One himself, despite being four-armed as well.
The army of the enemies was turned away like a newlywed woman overcome with trepidation;
yet the goddess Lakṣmī remained clinging to the chest of that warrior, as bold and intensely passionate as a willing servant.
Let the sins of even the most cruel-hearted remain, for the minds of the virtuous are ever steadfast.
He forcibly drew toward himself those who were naturally turbid and base, just as a magnet attracts iron filings.
During his journey upon the ocean, a row of ships laden with white sandalwood appeared beautiful,
like a flight of swans spread across the interior of the sea by the force of the Ganges' current and led along on all sides.
He made the Earth— whose garments were the waves of the ocean, whose girdle was the shimmering rows of ripples formed by the clusters of jewels tossed up by that water,
whose broad hips were the mountain slopes, and whose face was the spotless moon— as if she were a devoted woman, bringing her delight.
His praise is [the song] of his fame, which has spread throughout the three worlds.
Though emaciated by asceticism, he carried the Gaṅgā like Bhagīratha;
though full of a multitude of syllables, he joined them to the action within a single word;
and though knowing elision, augmentation, and modification, he employed words free from elision, augmentation, and modification.
That which is perceivable like a pillar and so forth...

[125ab] But that which is perceivable as non-existent, being absolutely free from defects, is like the horn of a hare. [125cd] The apprehension of a person in a post is a false cognition; this is also the case regarding other things. [126ab]
In whom there arose the most profound and perfect knowledge;
who, leading both policy and valor to the state of being the birthplace of illustrious fame,
bore [the burden] like the splendor of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ for that [knowledge].

He who was powerful, heroic, handsome, and rich in wisdom became like a single portion of the five sons of Pāṇḍu. Nakula was handsome; Sahadeva knew the science of astrology... (as seen on Wikipedia in the *Bhārata*).
Once Śiva had been directly perceived, he became peaceful and fulfilled in his duty toward the protection of the earth;
he made his hand, which was joined with the enemy of the Dānavas, like his mind.
Desiring, as it were, to perform the rites of the Aśvamedha sacrifice again and again, he [acted].
Even today, he sends forth his horse of glory, which cannot be seized by any quarter,
produced through statesmanship and remaining unknown to his enemies until it is ready to bear fruit;
just as Kuntī [concealed] her brother Karṇa, so too has he [concealed] this undertaking, which Arjuna has now destroyed.
While they beheld him, who dwelt in their minds and surpassed all things in beauty,
the status of being "mind-born" for the bodiless god [Kāma] was rendered obsolete.
When his qualities were sung in a vast multitude of verses by the thousand-pathed [Veda], [the world was moved].
The hearing of other qualities is stilled by the memory of her, like a melody in a *sāman* chant.
For her fame—born of her beauty—is fixed in the hearts of excellent women, engraved there as dear letters by the desire for her splendor. (133cd–134)
He who, by means of the fourteen branches of knowledge,
like the Creator through the various stages of cosmic manifestation, maintained the stability of the world;
even a small portion of the earth which had been sprinkled with the waters of his consecration— 135–136ab.
He removed the distress of the sovereign of all the earth from every land.
The mere placement of his feet was upon the jeweled throne,
whereas the burden of you rests upon the heads of the kings of the earth.
Upon whose head shone a single white parasol,
appearing like the orb of the full moon moving near to serve as a comparison for his face;
whom Gaurī, seeing that she shared half of Hara’s body, seemed to regard with jealousy.
Śrī, her limbs clinging to him, embraced the Lord, thinking, "May I become like this.
Though his nature is pure, it is colored [by her];
nevertheless, he is thoroughly known and remains free from any mixture of castes.
Placing before him his two priests, who were as fiery as fire itself, the skillful king entered the assembly hall—he who was like a third fire between them.
He, though a single teacher, was sung of as such; yet, with light punishments, he governed his subjects.
As if rebuking Dharmarāja, who wields the fierce rod of punishment,
Dharma— once four-footed— has been rendered crippled by Kali, leaving it with but a single foot,
as if by one who knows the eighteen branches of learning were to reduce it to a mere eighteen parts.
Even at night, while performing his daily rites, he remained free from attachment to worldly affairs; for him, who was innocent of even the slightest appearance of fault,
the autumn season— though possessing Indra’s bow— seemed as if it were without Indra’s bow.
He was impelled by the rays of the red jewels upon the heads of the bowing kings;
though he had set out for world conquest, being stirred up by his own power, he— who,
despite possessing manifest and pure goodness (sattva), produced darkness through passion (rajas).

In the act of withdrawal, as if thinking "I have been scorched by him," the Earth, out of anger, became dust for the creation of Śrī and covered his chariot with it. Although their brilliance was equal, the fire-bannered god [Agni] made smoke his banner, while he [Rāma] made the sun his banner. (147ab–148ab)
He who seized that blazing splendor, which was attended by invincible victories; whose army increased even in autumn as it had in the rainy season;
and who, through mere sport, shattered the kings who obstructed his path.
Having shattered the enemy formation protected by the wheels, he entered it like Garuḍa entering the domain of Indra, desiring to seize the nectar of victory;
surpassing the lords of the lunar mansions— the stars of the warrior class— with his splendor.
Mounted upon the sky that was the field of battle, he shone like the risen sun;
shaking his loudly twanging bow, he himself appeared like the science of archery incarnate, demonstrating the excellence of his training in the art of the bow.
He by whom arrows were released from the twanging sound of the bowstring drank the honey of blood from the lotus-faces of his enemies in battle; he whose sword-blade,
smeared with blood, was embraced by the severed arms of his foes.
It shone like the flame of a snake-sacrifice fire, with hundreds of falling serpents;
seeing his sword-like form, the enemies, as if perceiving the time of their own death,
plunged into it with the hope that it was the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī.
He who, like the awakened Indra, shattered with the thunderbolt of his arm the mountain-like enemies who had caused him grievous harm and were rushing forward with the speed of a rising tide; he who,
though skilled in all systems of justice, was a peerless hero in every battle.
He who abandoned both right and wrong conduct as if they were equal, according to the logic of the lion’s glance (siṃhāvalokita-nyāya);
by him, with his brandishing sword, the head of an enemy was severed in battle with great force,
and it followed his own inner self that had ascended to heaven, as if leaping upward.
He who was exceedingly radiant, being colored by the weapons of the glorious enemy,
like Mount Meru which is naturally luminous with the rays of its jewels;
he by whom the Goddess of Victory was firmly established upon the edge of his sword.
Nourishing abundant desires, she increased the prosperity of her progeny;
indeed, her victorious fame, having pervaded the earth, now extends to heaven, as if to set aside the ill-repute formerly brought upon Indra by Indrajit.

He struck the row of women’s breasts as if it were Śrī’s disheveled braid, with his sword-blade acting like a blue lotus; he seemed to be refuting the doctrine that "all conditioned things are impermanent" by displaying a string of pearls within its opening petals.
He constantly maintained his own glory, refined by his prowess;
even his beloved wife, though bold as a man, led him into the act of battle,
just as Lakṣmī, who yearns for no other, leads the unborn one [Viṣṇu] to the moon-like Sunanda.
The Creator, out of joy, surely bestowed upon him— whose very appearance was capable of destroying the world’s afflictions—
the eternal splendor of Kāma,
so that he might, as it were, desire to know the extent and course of his fame throughout the three worlds.
"Even now he goes about with his hand outstretched...
(166cd). 'The moon suffers a loss of digits due to a quarrel with a woman,' so indeed did Hara say;
for there, having been diligently disciplined and freed from envy, the Earth, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī [reside]. (167ab-167cd)
Does *kalāhāni* also mean *kāntihāni* (loss of luster)?
[He was one] who, with the blazing fires from the tusks of lordly elephants severed by his sword, created ten million torches for the Goddess of Victory on the battlefield at night. (168)

His command, which promotes the increase of his subjects, revolves sleeplessly, as if by mere remembrance, like the enemy of the Daityas when the universe has been withdrawn. Having initiated himself for the sacrifice of battle, he shattered the circle of his enemies.

Although he had attained the state of freedom from disease, he still cherished his beloved, the Goddess of Victory (Jayaśrī). Bhīmasena, who was capable of crossing the dense forests of mountains, sought out the lotus-like wealth [of the earth] and brought about the sovereignty over the quarters of the world,
which was filled with the disheveled tresses of the ruined city of Alakā.
The fame of him, which even now does not fade—
[as if] joined by drops of nectar clinging to Mount Mandara—
by whom, in battle, the severed heads of enemies rose up in the sky with their crowns intact. (172–173ab)
The hosts of divine women who sing his glory have surely been granted ornaments;
for the gods, their strength exhausted by crossing the shoreless ocean of his fame,
have surely found rest upon the sandy banks of the peaks of the Golden Mountain.

His command shone upon the head of the mountain-king like the radiance of the sun, possessing the supernatural power of a blooming lotus and crushing the darkness of his enemies. Śrī, who had resided upon the blue-lotus-like chest of the Ocean, was taken away by Śrīdhara.
O Śrīpriyā, he by whom the glory and fortune of King Yaśas was [bestowed] upon the lotus-like faces of the quarters;
he who, though bearing the luster of a lotus in his eye, the earth in his hand, and Śrī upon his chest,
is yet proclaimed as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
Bearing a crest-jewel that crushed the mountains and was adorned with shimmering gems,
his chest shone like that of Viṣṇu— the abode of Śrī and Rati.
With a towering height adorned by a vast, radiant orb, he appeared exceedingly brilliant.
That king of kings, who by his majesty did not overstep the established order of Meru;
who, having brought about the defeat of Duryodhana’s enemy with ease,
protected the sovereignty of Dharmarāja, now free from all thorns.
By him, Śrīdhara, the jewel of fame obtained from churning the ocean of battle throughout the three worlds was scattered away for the sake of no other purpose than his own;
he who [bestowed] that which is beloved by the three worlds, whose eyes are the ever-moving moon and sun.
... with these [words] he caused him to drink from his own hand.
(182cd) Even though the wish-fulfilling tree that is his feet bestows all desires, it did not grant him prosperity.
(183ab) For toward a haughty enemy, generosity is what accomplishes submission to a lord. (183cd)
Ah, how difficult it is to abandon one's own nature,

since Fortune— who for a moment after a moment steals away the joy from the hearts of her enemies— is here made motionless upon his chest! She is like the full moon seized by Rāhu, or like the god of love consumed by fire.
Beauty resides swiftly in her lotus-face, and fearlessness dwells within her body.
For this much alone, even he who is a scholar of grammar (śābdika) is called by the wise "one who knows the word apada" (apadajña);
for he never said to the multitude of beggars, "There is nothing."
He who once conquered the pride of Kama with his organ of sight alone,
yet always remained unconquered by all the senses;
he who surpassed the power, intellect, and progress of others through his own great successes.

By him, the three qualities—rajas, sattva, and tamas—were deposited in three [objects] for the perfect accomplishment of the primary virtues of the earth, the ocean, and Mount Meru: patience, profundity, and fortitude;
rajas was placed in his military expedition, sattva in his righteousness, and tamas in the hearts of his enemies.
Free from envy, though dwelling in the forest, he was like an ascetic even while ruling as a sovereign;
no one failed to attain liberation, for they were terrified of him as if they were afraid of cyclic existence (bhava).
Making the forest a city of enemies and making the enemy’s city a forest, [he acted]. 190–191ab.
He who, like the word *iti*, brought about a reversal of the meaning of things—
[he] whose face, upon seeing the risen full moon, caused his enemies to remember [their own] mouths;
[and] by whose moonlight the rocks on the mountain were scorched, even though the stone surface was cool.
Devoted to Śrīkaṇṭha and bearing the burden of the leadership of the circle [of vassals],
he— who was broad-hipped, tall, and firm— shone like his own arm;
he [attained] the removal of faults, the excellence of virtues, and the auspicious destiny of those born of noble lineage.
He drew his bow in the circle of the natural disposition (prakṛtimaṇḍala) as if it were a circle of a bow;
even the orb of the moon-king appeared as if its deer-enemy had been slain by the waters of tears shed by his beloved.
If the fame and valor of those slain are sung by the throngs of celestial nymphs—
charming, heart-piercing, and like the command of the God of Love to wandering women—
then the sun, through its restraint and favor, follows the two paths of the north and the south.
He who, having passed through the transition between those two in a state of equanimity,
completed the sacrifice of battle with the wealth seized from his enemies,
began— like the learned Yudhiṣṭhira— a Vedic ritual.
The prosperity of his subjects was greater for him who did not abandon the worship of the gods;
whereas for Dilīpa, there had previously been a loss of subjects because he abandoned that [worship].
For him, the entire circle of the earth seemed as if it had attained contact with the sacrificial fires.
The sun, desiring to seize its portion of the oblation, was hidden and obscured by the smoke [of his sacrifices].
(200cd) His rain of gifts, consisting of all kinds of jewels, is constant and golden;
whereas the rain of the showerer Indra is momentary, released from the clouds, and consists of lightning. (201ab–201cd)
Although submerged in a single ocean of charity, his earth— though ablaze with the fires of sacrifice—
shone forth as it stood in its central expanse;
he made the entire kingdom free of tears, for the kings bowed before him.
May Hara endure within himself that flow of tears for his father-in-law;
he who, like the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, dispelling the fear of exhaustion from three strides,
traversed the entire world again with but a single stride.
Endowed with the qualities of the sun and moon— scorching and gladdening respectively— and accompanied by their rays,
he is to be venerated by practitioners like the rising of the twilight, because he is not to be transgressed.
He is one for whom the common misconception that takes what is not that to be that is generally to be abandoned.
Because he grasped virtues as if they were jewels, even though they were offered by one who had been reduced to misfortune—
just as Mārīca was seized by Rāma upon hearing his name and other single syllables—
the heroic king of his enemies was struck with a fear that could not be surpassed.
Like the Lord of Śārṅga and Umā, who disregard the joint where their own bodies are joined in various forms,
those two created him of such a kind with only half [of themselves].
For he was not only peerless in the arrangement of words, but even in the arrangement of syllables.
He is not merely comparable [to Kāma] by the technical rule of "capacity" (samartha-paribhāṣā),
for he has conquered Kāma not only through his physical beauty but even by his noble birth— Kāma, who increases the seed of the worlds and extends protection from injury.
He who, by the duty of a kṣatriya, defeated Sudakṣiṇā while she was accepting gifts at Dilīpa’s sacrifice, yet bestowed her upon worthy recipients;
he by whom benevolence— the peerless ornament— was preserved.
The jewel named Kaustubha alone is dear to the chest of Nārāyaṇa.
Having approached Dadhīca with a harsh voice, she was cursed;
yet, having returned to heaven, she was granted a blessing by Sarasvatī with a melodious voice, which she still possesses today on this earth.

His valor was a rival to that of others, and even his fame— though neuter— is renowned for being "attached" to the women who are the quarters of the sky, as if it had taken on their gender. His enemy, unable to win Sītā, remained devoted instead to Maṇḍodarī.
The night-stalker Rāvaṇa-like one, an enemy of the illustrious Āditya,
while seemingly refuting through reasoning the doctrine of a void self (anātmavāda),
established the all-pervading majesty of the Self everywhere.
He alone, possessing innumerable virtues, appeared as if wishing to conquer the sophists, as it were declaring the distinction between qualities and the possessor of qualities.
Not only is the earth made fragrant by those who possess sweet scents; (217–218ab)

Even the sky was deprived of its qualities by his fame, which overspread the entire circle of the quarters. Like a suffix applied after a prefix to a verbal root, he who was learned in the scriptures composed a verse for the sake of conveying meaning against his enemy.
He was the father of Yaśas-candra, who spread his fame throughout the ten directions;
followed by Anasūyā, he shone like another Atri.
Though devoted to the meaning of the Purāṇas, he was also fond of the speech of the elders.
In this captivating poem, the ninefold meaning alone has been sought by someone;
though Śiva is partless (niṣkala), he is eternally attached to him who,
when made manifest (sakalīkṛta), attained every single digit, yet the half-moon did not do so out of dullness.
Indeed, all the exaltation belongs to him whose virtuous qualities have been thus described;
for even his face was then cast down under the pretext of modesty.
Indeed, he was surpassed only by Kārttikeya, who bears the form of a youth.
He attained a youth that was free from old age and had never been reached before;
he caused all his subjects to follow instructions that turned away from what should not be done,
so that they might abundantly promote each other's welfare and well-being.
Having set aside the entire task previously performed by others,
he, being skillful, accomplished that which was prescribed by the scriptures— something new and uncreated by others—
which, upon attainment, is endowed with merit, free from negative consequences, and adorned with the splendor of fame.
The fame of kings has perished like the Gaṅgā into the matted locks of Śiva.
Even his fame is not repeated twice merely for the sake of constant iteration, though it is recounted countless times by devoted poets without any sense of weariness.

By this much may he be inferred: that warrior, the best among those skilled in weapons, who with the edge of his sword cut down his enemy like the bodiless god of love (Anaṅga) together with his limbs;
from whom, Dakṣa, Medhā, and the other ten were born as the sons of Prajāpati.
They remained steadfastly devoted solely to the Dharma of ten limbs.
Having seen her beauty again and again in former times, two gods said to Purūravas: "All those [beauties] of yours have now become diminished."
As if to attain the status of Dharmarāja by dragging away the buffalo of Yama,
his beloved queen, the Earth, always followed after him toward the southern quarter.
While he was ruling the kingdom, it was free from thieves.
The heart of a woman was captivated by a certain glance of his.
Though he was constantly immersed in the nectar-ocean of the elders' instructions,
he set foot upon the violation of the dignity of the most excellent of elder kings.
He who is liberated from rajas and tamas, endowed with all auspicious qualities,
and who is considered the Supreme Puruṣa beyond even primordial nature (prakṛti) and the intellect (buddhi);
he for whom hundreds of thousands of oblations have been poured by officiating priests into the sacrificial fire of the Lakṣahoma.
Like a seed sown in water, it produced a great fruit.
In ancient times, the Sūta and the Māgadha, being urged, praised Pṛthu;
indeed, this entire world praises him spontaneously by its very nature.

The mountains bow down to him under the pretext of having their wings clipped, as if out of fear of losing their own mountain-hood when he, the bearer of the earth, is bent low and destroyed [by his enemies]. Śrī Someśvara Bhaṭṭa and others learned Mīmāṃsā from that twice-born man.
He studied under wise men who had explained the meaning of the Vedas and were devoted to Brahman.
Even today, the "Royal Pathway" (Rājapaddhati) composed by him shines forth;
by following it, kings have attained both worlds, endowed with welfare.
He who, by his stainless nature, did not even rival the moon,
which day and night possesses a full orb free from partiality; he, though having reached a state of impotence, brought prosperity to his subjects through his sovereignty.
His conduct shone, having conquered the lords of his enemies, like that of Arjuna; Lakṣmī,
who was whirled about during the churning for nectar through the confusion of the Mandara mountain,
became firmly established upon him, as if she had reached the unswerving golden Meru.
By him, even within the small cavity of the universe, a vast fame was displayed,
just as the all-powerful Kṛṣṇa revealed the three worlds within the hollow of his mouth;
[he did so] through the policy of his priest Vāgīśa, who was like the city of Śiva’s conch.

He who, like the wielder of the thunderbolt, governed Amarāvatī after the lords of the enemies of the gods had been quelled; he who made even that fortress difficult to traverse within the circle of his foes;
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva indeed render Meru an abode that cannot be destroyed.
While he ruled, the qualities [of nature] became subordinate among the elements;
even their reversal was of great prosperity.
In the lake of his empire, the lotus of his glory—fragrant with fame and possessing the filaments of royal fortune—was in full bloom.
His lotus-feet shone, graced by the bees that were kings;
he who softened the countless weapons of his enemies in battle,
while Hara, however, was rendered soft by the flower-arrowed god whose sole weapon is a flower.
The fame of him who punishes those deserving of punishment shines unbroken,
like the orb of the moon risen from the ocean of the non-punishment of those not deserving of punishment;
it appears as if intoxicated by the water of the gift of hundreds of elephants bestowed during his extensive sacrifice.
His fame still wanders throughout the three worlds even today. Even Kamalā, though fond of lotuses, abandoned the thorn-filled lotus and went instead to his lotus-like arm, which is free from thorns.
Requested by Brahmā, he who was already pure became even more purified as Śiva;
though his color was like that of pure crystal, he again became blue-and-red (nīlalohita).
By the fire of his majesty, he consumed even those situated within the army.
How much more so those enemies who have fled into the depths of the wood?
The Supreme Person alone was sleeping in the single ocean;
yet now, many are awakened by the hymns of praise within that single ocean of his fame.
Even for his praise, poetry— which follows as a natural consequence of the efforts of poets—
does not fade like the Veda, owing to its contact with the nectar of his deeds.
While Bhīṣaṇa was terrifying her, the Earth, being afraid, assigned a certain task to Pṛthu.

Having given much milk to others, he gave everything to that one who grants fearlessness; his conduct, directed toward the fulfillment of the welfare of others by abandoning concern for his own interest,
was adorned with capability like the compound (samāsa) and other grammatical figures.

The term *ekārthībhāvasāmarthya* means that in the five types of *vṛtti*, there is the capacity for *ekārthībhāva*. For example, in the compound *rājapuruṣaḥ*, the words together express a single integrated meaning. This is contrasted with *vyapekṣāsāmarthya*, where meanings are related through mutual expectancy; if *ekārthībhāvasāmarthya* is present, you cannot add qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) to the constituent parts. Thus, one cannot say *vṛddhasya rājamātaṅgaḥ*.

His activity, adorned by the power of unifying meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) like a compound (*samāsa*), proceeds by means of the radiant knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is the cause for attaining liberation;
yet, even though he is thus endowed, he is never separated from the hearts of men. (259)

Hara, the Lord of the Universe, who— though free from desire for the possessions of others and though being a generous donor— bestowed the quality of passion (rajas) as prosperity upon only one part of his own body, yet bestowed the quality of goodness (sattva) upon all seven parts. He possesses such skill [in this].
He was not capable of giving his own [wealth] to another, yet he took only that which belonged to others.
There was doubt among other warriors as to whether there would be victory or defeat;
but with him, victory alone was certain in every battle.
He who, in battle, struck down the cruel Śrīrahas with his two breasts;
he whose chest crushed the tips of the tusks of the elephants of his vanquished enemies;
he who was victorious amidst showers of flowers scattered by the hands of the inhabitants of heaven.
Like a warrior in competition, he scattered clusters of blossoms from the garden of his fame;
as if binding an unprecedented ornament upon the fragmented world,
he bestowed thousands of unbroken moons of glory throughout every direction.
The bee-like eye, clinging to the fruit of beauty upon the body of the mango tree of men, is unable to depart, being drawn by the flowers of his fame;
as if desiring to proclaim himself the Lord, he provides the very cause for such a claim. (266–267)
Remaining indifferent toward his own nature, the virtuous king performed what was to be done.
He caused those kings, such as Śrīndravarmā and Śrīyaśovarmā,
who had been established by him in their respective positions, to remain steadfast in their shares of the sacrifice that he had ordained.
In the Yaśodhara lake created by the illustrious Yaśovarman,
the accomplished [king] made even the unseen Dharma manifest to the eyes; he who,
upon the earth which is like a conch shell, [established] the gods and the self-existent ones.
Having become the sole sacrificer among those established [in that office], he increased their worship.
Just as the splendor of the mandala was bestowed upon Bhadreśvara by that moon among kings,
so did it increase, spotless as if out of joy to put to shame the beauty of the moon itself.

Having conquered the lord of Campā by the strength of his arms, he took away that king's fortune for Hari, as if desiring to bestow upon the Self-born Lord at the bank of the Viṣṇupadī the title of "Lord of Campā. He offered three gates to the celestial river, which had made her dwelling on the banks of the white-flowing Gaṅgā.

As if saying, "Let these go by way of the triple path according to their names," that golden city, along with its vast enjoyments, was filled with dharma, artha, and kāma— though it remained beyond the senses— just as the son of Satyavatī, having composed the *Bhārata-saṃhitā*, completed it with the three Vedas.
The petition of King Yaśovarman was as devoid of substance as the *vijñapti* (representation) taught by the Yogācāras;
yet, by him—who was resolute in upholding his own duty—it was rendered meaningful, like the three Vedas (*trayī*).
Though the mountain peaks of pride belonging to other submerged kings were shattered, he here possesses the height of a lotus in this lake. 275–276ab.
That very Viṣṇu, having transcended the world, established his station, as radiant as the solar orb;
that is this preeminent Liṅga here, known as Śrī Rājendra Bhadreśvara,
which is graced by these four beautiful images of Gaurī, Śaurī, and Īśvara.

In the Śaka year [1098], when the sky was illuminated by the eight radiant fires whose bodies are flames, he established this Lord Śrī Rājendravarmeśvara, who was endowed with the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, by means of four upward-facing faces that were as bright as the cheerful countenance of a joyful Śambhu when speaking of his own glory.

For his own prosperity, he [established] the status of a sovereign king by means of the eight [deities] beginning with Indra, as if they were his very self, situated in the directions starting from the southeast (Agni).
Even though he was already a lord of universal form like Rājendra Viśvarūpa, Hari, who possesses a universal appearance and is captivating,
was fashioned by him here as if he were a mass of pure splendor for the three worlds.
Having brought glory to the victory of his own mother Jayadevī, the consort of the illustrious King Harṣadeva,
he established here Girijā, the younger sister of his mother.
He was the lord of kings, Rājendravarman, a sovereign among rulers of the earth.
He brought about the prosperity of King Śrī Harṣavarman’s younger brother by fashioning twelve internal liṅgas, as beautiful as the stars beginning with Śārṅgī;
these were like the eight forms of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva) themselves, appearing as if the thick streams of nectar spat from the moon upon his head had solidified.

Just as the Fortune of the Three Worlds is attended by the eight guardians of the quarters who have attained royal status, so too was various wealth bestowed upon these deities by that king gathered together. In this [temple], he provided an ocean-like abundance, dense with heaps of jewels and golden ornaments.

May the ritual for the worship of the gods, accompanied by the surging sound of musical instruments, proceed without transgressing its appointed time. By that Indra, through the clouds appointed as his servants, may the divine oblation— consisting of water like celestial food, containing the six flavors according to the requirements of the recipient, and being the sole essence of their own duty— be offered.
The future King of Kambuja, the generous Śrī Rājendravarman, is well known;
he entreats you with these noble words: "May you protect this, your own dharma.
For this very self, though one, is divided manifold within the body as both the agent and the enjoyer.
Therefore, may you wise ones grasp your own duty as all dharmas flourish for you.

(287cd) Even that distinction of agents which is imagined through the difference of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) in order to differentiate the fruits of actions—that distinction is merely figurative (*bhākta*). It is to be pierced by the realization of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), just as darkness is dispelled by the light of the sun. (288)
The earth has been acquired by you through ascetic penance;
whatever exists upon it, all of this must be protected without even a moment’s neglect, lest it be oppressed by others.
This definition of a Kṣatriya—“one who protects from injury”—has been proclaimed to you by the Lotus-born Creator from his own arm.
May it illuminate its own purpose for those who possess progeny and who bear the great ornament of the prowess of their arms.
When dharma might perish even amidst the prosperity of the pleasures of sovereignty for those joined with sleep,
may that awakening be for the sake of its restoration, like the milk in the ocean of Nārāyaṇa.
Since for this reason the Lord Viṣṇu, though unborn, became the son of Aditi and was subject to womanhood,
and Śiva likewise went to the lotus-born Brahmā— may that [example] be for you the preservation of the established order of dharma.
May she, who is embraced by Yama (restraint) and delights in niyamas (observances), be as dear to Satyavat as Rāmā herself.

Bestowing upon you a blind vision regarding my body of fame—which has righteousness as its life-breath—what man would desire to seize this divine property, such as the jewels, which is merely an ornament and yet like poison?
Such is the firm conviction of the wise: that it is like the Kālakūṭa poison residing in the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha. (293cd–294)
May you long possess your kingdom, being devoted to righteousness and preeminent in the virtue of renunciation—
surpassing in splendor and endowed with the prosperity of treasury and military force, like the ancient kings beginning with Karandhama.
This maiden, seeking a husband, has found in one such as you a worthy consort, just as a noble-born girl finds a husband of her own station.
Modesty and gentleness cause my own request to reveal its true nature.
This speech of mine, the sole path to heaven, liberation, and tranquility, is a garland upon the head of the Lord.
May it, like the Mandākinī entering the ocean, deeply gladden your minds.
For those who desire death, this prayer has been rightly spoken by the wise for the attainment of their desired goal;
having followed that which leads to immortality, it is for the sake of increasing the Dharma. (298ab)
Therefore, I request that which is desired by me through my passion for the Dharma. 298cd
